title: Tracewalk: client-observed latency vs cost across batching modes (draft)
content:
Summary:

This note records a small, targeted benchmark we ran using a "tracewalk" approach: take representative customer request traces (mixed prompt lengths, chat-state sizes), and replay them through the serving stack while toggling batching modes. The goal: compare client-observed latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99) and estimated per-1M-token cost for three modes we commonly consider for production: no-batching, auto-batch (short windows), and continuous batching (long-running assembly/batching pipeline).

Why 'tracewalk' here: synthetic throughput runs are useful, but they miss request heterogeneity and KV cache dynamics. Tracewalk replays a short stream of realistic customer traffic (5000 requests, sampled from recent prod traces) so we capture inter-request timing, prefix reuse, and cache priming.

Environment and test knobs:
- HW: 1x A100-80GB per pod (gpu type: a100-80).
- Model: open-llama-13b (fp16), standard KV cache enabled.
- Runtime build: serving-runtime@main (commit sha in linked PR).
- Network: intra-region (us-west2) — no cross-region routing in this run.
- Workload: 5k requests sampled from two customers (chat-like and single-shot completion). Request mix: 60% short (<=64 tokens), 30% medium (65-256), 10% long (256-1024).
- Batching modes tested:
  * no-batch: each request dispatched immediately to a worker.
  * auto-batch: 5ms assembly window, up to 16 items.
  * continuous: request-assembly pipeline keeps a standing batch (up to 64), opportunistically filling for 20ms windows.

Methodology:
- Warmup: 1k-request warmup (same trace but different slice).
- Each mode was run 3x; results below are median across repeats.
- Measurement capture: client-observed end-to-end time (request send -> final token received). Server-side logs used to tag per-stage times (assembly, queue-wait, kernel-step, grpc serialization).
- Cost estimate: backend GPU time * price per-GPU-hour (use internal rate $3.50/hr for A100 pool) converted to per-1M-token cost using total tokens produced during the run. This is a crude, comparable metric (excludes infra egress and control-plane costs).

Results (median of repeats):

ASCII table (latency in ms; cost in $ per 1M tokens):

Mode         | p50  | p95  | p99  | mean-assembly-ms | mean-queue-ms | est-cost-1Mtok
-------------|------|------|------|------------------|---------------|---------------
no-batch     | 18   | 72   | 185  | 0                | 6             | 3.95
auto-batch   | 12   | 56   | 140  | 4.6              | 10            | 3.15
continuous   | 14   | 40   | 88   | 12.2             | 18            | 2.62

Quick observations on the numbers above:
- Continuous batching shows the lowest p95/p99 cost per token (2.62$) because steady batches improve GPU utilization and amortize kernel startup.
- p50 favors auto-batch here because short-window batching reduces added assembly latency for small immediate requests while capturing a decent batch hit-rate for medium requests.
- p99 is where continuous manifests the largest win (185 -> 88 ms) relative to no-batch, indicating fewer long tail spikes when the pipeline can smooth peaks.

Representative stage breakdown (continuous mode, p99 slice):
- client-network: 10 ms
- assembly: 24 ms
- queue-wait (batch fill): 34 ms
- kernel-exec: 14 ms
- postprocess/serialize: 6 ms
Total ~ 88 ms

Mini ASCII bar chart (p99 normalized, lower is better):
no-batch   : ################################################# (185)
auto-batch : ############################### (140)
continuous : ################### (88)

Why costs differ more than raw p50:
- GPU utilization: continuous mode increased GPU token throughput by ~35% because it reduced tiny-kernel overheads and improved tensor packing. That lowered the per-token GPU time and thus cost.
- Overhead shift: continuous pushes some latency into assembly + queue waiting; when traffic is steady, this is amortized. For bursty traffic, queue waits can spike if assembly windows are not tuned.

Key qualitative takeaways:
- For interactive, latency-sensitive customer-facing endpoints with strict p50 SLAs, auto-batching with a very small assembly window (~3-6ms) looks best — it gives good p50 while improving cost moderately.
- For throughput-first internal pipelines (ingestion, embeddings, batch rerank), continuous batching yields cheaper per-token cost and better tail behavior.
- The tail (p99) benefit of continuous mode suggests it is a good default for high-concurrency tenants where long tails hurt SLOs.

Tradeoffs and risk notes:
- Increased queue-wait under continuous mode can blow up p99 for very sparse traffic patterns (we saw this when we artificially throttled requests to 1 rps). Need a traffic-aware fallback to no-batch if inter-arrival jumps above a threshold.
- Cache priming: tracewalk showed that medium-length prefix reuse amplifies the advantage of batching modes that co-locate similar KV cache entries; different customer mixes will change the delta.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q: how do results change on L4/T4-like cheaper GPUs? (TODO: schedule run on test L4 pool; ticket ENG-3498).
- Q: can we improve continuous mode assembly so that it dynamically adapts window size based on instantaneous arrival rate? (design spike needed).
- TODO: Add network jitter emulation (we used intra-region low-lat runs only). Need cross-region traces.
- TODO: Export per-route cost deltas to console so product can make routing decisions (see linked PR for initial wire-up).

Recommended next steps:
1) Run the same tracewalk on cheaper GPU families and on a 2x model size (to observe kernel startup sensitivity). Owner: Alex Duarte, target: 2026-06-18.
2) Prototype an adaptive-assembly scheduler: window size adjusts with short-term arrival rate. Small spike experiment + microbench. Owner: Zoe Wang.
3) Add a simple fallback rule in router: if measured inter-arrival > X for 100ms, prefer no-batch to keep p50 steady for foreground flows. Chat ops to define X.

Appendix: raw numbers (median of 3 runs)
- total tokens produced: no-batch: 1.23M, auto-batch: 1.25M, continuous: 1.29M
- total GPU-hours consumed: no-batch: 0.112 hr, auto-batch: 0.095 hr, continuous: 0.083 hr
- notes on reproducibility: full run script and seed are in linked_artifacts (GH PR). Re-run flags: --tracewalk-seed=20260608 --sample-slice=0.2 --warmup=1000

Notes to self: Save a short slide deck of the three modes (p50/p95/p99 + cost) for next weekly runtime sync. Also circle back to product to align on default routing policy for new tenants.

End of note.
